records.title: Show HN: erXos – a microkernel OS in Erlang based on Genera/Plan 9/QNX ideas
records.author: stass
records.storyText:
What if every Erlang process were an operating-system process? With as much system code and drivers written in Erlang itself. This is something I was pondering for a while, and finally was able to prototype thanks to AI coding agents.

erXos is a capability-based microkernel OS in Erlang: drivers, filesystems, and the network stack are all supervised Erlang processes, same as any app.

The kernel itself is Fiasco, in C++, slightly modified for erXos needs. This is an OS I wanted for a long time: an Erlang machine where every BEAM process is a process visible to the OS and scheduler, not something bolted on top.

You can try it right now with nothing to install: there is an emulator on the website that boots the whole OS in the browser ARM64 emulator. At the rc prompt, try `ps`, `top`, `ping` or `erl` and write any kind of erlang code. There's a Pi 4 SD image and a QEMU image too. The goal is to build an ultra-reliable microkernel OS with hot code loading and both system and BEAM-based isolation. The latter is one thing that would allow you to run millions of processes on the system, something that would be prohibitive on a microkernel alone due to the context switch overhead. Capabilities keep every component least-privileged, supervision keeps the machine running when drivers or subsystems crash, and hot code loading would let you fix a broken driver without reboot.

The secondary goal is to keep as much of a UNIX face as possible. Too many novel OSes change things for no particular reason that makes them hard to use. erXos tries to preserve as many existing UNIX/FreeBSD concepts as much as possible to remove the learning curve.

What works today:

- Boots in the browser/v64, in QEMU, and on a Raspberry Pi 4 from an SD card

- A real shell (plan9 rc) with job control, pipes, `ps`, `grep`. It feels like UNIX on the surface

- Erlang versions of basic UNIX apps.

- Drivers written in Erlang: UART, virtio, SD card, Ethernet (GENET), display

- A pure Erlang EROFS filesystem for root images

- A TCP/IP stack in Erlang based on FreeBSD network stack and verified for correctness against it

- Domains: every app runs as its own address space or Erlang node, isolated from others

- Plan 9 namespaces and 9P everywhere; windows are files like RIO and 9P is a file protocol between OS servers

- Supervision end to end: if a driver fails, its supervisor resets the device and restarts it

I also have 2 demo apps built on app sdk: a full-screen kiosk app with live crypto quotes and clock and, of course Doom, which ships on the Pi 4 card image (type `doom`).

What's coming:

- Raspberry Pi 5 support

- Full display on the Pi

- WIFI

- Bluetooth

- POSIX-lite for C programs, so existing code can run as a domain

- Performance, debugging and tracing features.

The code is all available under the BSD license.

Would love to hear all and any feedback!

records.title: Show HN: Dayfile.app – Append-only log for your scripts and agents
records.author: gilad
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm Gilad.

dayfile.app is a "git log for scripts and agents", with ordered history, append-only logging as foundational characteristics. The service is currently in beta, AGPL-licensed.

As I was looking at various ways to record and retrieve a day's to-dos, automation and operational outputs (update successes and failures), the idea of a running event log. dayfile.app's primary use case is DevOps tracking and event logging. Building this, I've emphasized simplifying posting - one HTTP request with a title and optional tags (used for filtering when reading the log), AI access via MCP server (an assistant can read, post or close to-dos) and self-hosting as a first-class citizen (`pip install dayfile`, SQLite database is local in this mode).

A demo is available at https://dayfile.app/demo. If using the cloud service and after generating a write token on the site, an example of posting an entry would be:

  curl -X POST https://USERNAME.dayfile.cloud/events \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer WRITE_TOKEN" \
  -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{"title":"Nightly backup finished","tags":["backup"]}'
To read back (filtering using tag):

  curl -H "Authorization: Bearer READ_TOKEN" \
  "https://USERNAME.dayfile.cloud/events?tag=backup&within=7d"
or paste https://USERNAME.dayfile.cloud/t/READ_TOKEN/f/backup.atom into a feed reader (you need to create a feed called `backup`).

What a local file can't do is notice something didn't happen - this is the heartbeat. dayfile.app can be configured to create an event if no associated event arrives. Imagine a backup which didn't run. A to-do event is created if no evidence of a successful backup shows up within a certain period. When the backup reports again, dayfile closes the associated to-do.

Current limits: logs are not end-to-end encrypted, sign-in is via GitHub only, the free beta allows 50,000 events and log size of 25MB. Pricing will be sorted out after this launch and as user feedback rolls in.

I'd love to hear in the comments on how you'd use it, what would prevent you from doing so, feature requests and suggestions. Bug reports can be submitted as issues on GitHub.

records.title: Show HN: Zeus – Claude Code for AI voice agents
records.author: kolchinski
records.storyText:
Hi everyone, Alex here - I’m one of the founders of ThunderPhone. We’re excited to announce the launch of Zeus, a platform that makes AI phone calls actually work without extensive hand-tuning!

You can see a head-to-head I made of the last version of ThunderPhone vs this one here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YlkIc3L29lo

A (somewhat long) summary:

When we started building business phone agents in 2024, we kept running into technical problems that ruined calls, caused by the limits of existing architectures. The two biggest issues were that phone agents misheard callers, and disobeyed scripts or responded in weird ways.

Both stemmed from the prevailing voice agent architecture - a “three-step” or “cascaded” pipeline: one transcription model turning caller audio into text, one LLM generating a response (and sometimes tool calls) from that text, and a TTS model turning response text into audio.

Transcription models aren’t perfect, especially in noisy environments, with unclear callers, in languages other than English, and on short utterances like “yeah”. With the pipeline approach, when caller audio is boiled down to a single “best guess” text transcript, mistakes are often unrecoverable: there’s typically no “top n” best guesses or other audio signal for the LLM to use if the transcript was wrong. That leads the LLM to respond to what the transcription model thought it heard instead of what the caller actually said.

The pipeline approach also caused weird responses and poor instruction-following due to the tradeoff between LLM speed and intelligence. Phone calls demand fast responses to feel natural, which is in tension with an LLM’s need to “think” and run inference - often for several seconds - to answer many prompts correctly. With a single LLM in the pipeline, the obvious choice is picking one fast enough to feel responsive, but that comes with an unavoidably high error rate on real calls, frustrating callers and sending calls off the rails.

More recently, end-to-end “speech-to-speech” models have won usage alongside three-step pipelines. They’re better at hearing callers correctly (though still not perfect), but they’re even worse at following instructions reliably, which is typically disastrous for business phone calls.

Once we understood these problems, we built our own stack to address them. Over the past year and a half, the ThunderPhone stack has largely solved mishearing and misbehaving by combining numerous models on each call.

For audio misunderstandings, we run multiple, even numerous, transcription models on most calls, giving more “shots on goal” from the original audio. Even if none gets it exactly right, multiple almost-correct answers let us triangulate on a correct transcript, using one or more LLMs to decide what the caller actually said. In challenging situations, we even pipe caller audio directly to one or more audio-input LLMs to further improve comprehension.

For instruction following, we run a mix of fast and slow LLMs on conversation turns to combine snappy responses with deeper thinking behind the scenes. In practice, this is a multi-staged classification problem: after 50ms, 500ms, 1s, etc., we simultaneously generate responses with increasing inference while classifying whether we need to “think harder” to generate a definitive correct answer.

Together with other smaller optimizations, these two approaches have been very effective. Qualitatively, customer calls go much more smoothly and reach successful outcomes far more frequently than on three-step or speech-to-speech pipelines. Quantitatively, we’ve set a record of 99.4% on the Big Bench Audio benchmark, smarter than any other model fast enough for real calls. (We’re also benchmarking ThunderPhone on more public benchmarks - stay tuned.)

The downside is configuration complexity. Every agent benefits from a different setup on the ThunderPhone stack, and even individual call turns on the same call often benefit from different stacks. Configuring this manually worked for enterprise customers, but made it prohibitive to give smaller self-serve customers the full benefits without giving their agents our full attention.

That’s how Zeus came about. Our enterprise configurations were repetitive enough that an AI could do them once we taught it how and gave it the right tools. We’re big fans of Claude Code and Codex for software development, but they fall short at configuring voice agents for a few reasons.

First, unlike software development, where you can compile code and run tests to verify things work, you can’t run live calls inside a computer right after configuring a voice agent - and coding agents don’t know how to run simulated calls out of the box, or “listen” to a call to spot real problems. We built both capabilities into Zeus, giving it a “closed loop” experience building, testing, and improving voice agents just like coding agents have with regular software.

Second, coding agents are pretty gullible about marketing claims. Companies building AI and voice infrastructure commonly post the most favorable possible interpretation of their capabilities online. Claude and Codex read those claims, believe them uncritically, and pick tools based on marketing rather than real performance. At best, that leads to suboptimal architectural choices; at worst, to voice agents that don’t really work at all.

We’ve sidestepped this with continuous evals feeding an internal knowledge base. For everything that matters for voice agents - accurate audio understanding, instruction following, noise cancelling, turn-taking, and more - we maintain internal benchmarks built on real call data. Every time a new AI model comes out, we (now mostly automatically) feed it through our evals for performance, speed, cost, and reliability/consistency. That feeds our internal knowledge base, which Zeus uses to pick the right stack for every agent, call, and conversation turn.

This all happens behind the scenes to keep the ThunderPhone experience seamless. A user just describes their use case and goals, and Zeus helps fill in ambiguities, connect VoIP and software integrations, and optimize the voice agent(s) on simulated and live calls until they hit the highest performance on business goals (conversions, unit economics, etc.) possible with today’s models.

Zeus is also differentiated on cost. Zeus itself is free to use for now, though we expect to move to subscription or token-based pricing later. For calls, we’ve become the first voice AI vendor to our knowledge to charge on a cost-plus basis: ThunderPhone customers pay exactly what we pay our vendors, plus a 17% margin on calls costing 2c/min or less, scaling linearly up to 25% for calls costing us 15c/min or more, and 25% from there on up.

However, we find that simple phone agents do well on a stack that costs about 2c/min, and more complex cases typically land around 5-10c/min - significantly cheaper than most alternatives.

Zeus is brand-new, so we’re eager to get feedback on how it works for customers, and any areas we could improve it. Give it a try and see what you think - let me know if you have any feedback or questions.

Alex

records.title: Show HN: Billet – 6MB (Agentic) Task Management System
records.author: skytrias
records.storyText:
Ever since AI has come, I've got worse at managing project tasks / goals. When you develop so fast now, things start lacking behind. For that reason I looked into creating a good set of skills I can use in any agent that support skills.

The result is billet-skills which you can find at https://github.com/Skytrias/billet-skills

Tasks are Markdown files with JSON frontmatter that live in docs/tasks/:

    ---
    { "id": 7, "title": "Add dark mode", "status": "ready", ... }
    ---
    ## Outcome
    The app follows the system's light or dark setting.
This allows me to create a bunch of tasks upfront and work on things more easily or in parallel.

Billet comes in two parts:

1. billet-skills, the skills: https://github.com/Skytrias/billet-skills

2. Billet, the viewer https://mktwsk.xyz/billet

Billet has a few ways of looking at the tasks in your project:

- List Mode

- Kanban Mode

- Plan Mode

Multiple Projects can be seen in the Home Dashboard and also a simple Timeline.

You can change the skills to whatever you like as long as it conforms to the format.

Other than that thats pretty much it. I've also got easy copy&paste support so it becomes easier saying "work on X and Y".

Billet is free - Give it a try and have fun! Feedback is welcome :)

Billet itself is closed-source though - as I have commercial projects that use the same UI core.

---

For those interested in the tech:

- Software Rendered UI, using Blend2D

- Custom immediate mode UI

- Custom platform layer

- Made in Odin

records.title: Show HN: GhostFleet: A Battleship game with an advanced AI opponent
records.author: anirbanhere
records.storyText:
Hi HN

I've always been drawn to puzzle and strategy games, and for a long time I've wanted to build a game of my own. While building my own version of battleship, I came across this idea of adding a super intelligent in-game AI which uses probability and statistics to reason with the board and fire its next shot.

The goal was to create a set of rules & logic capable of consistently outperforming human players, much like chess engines that have evolved to surpass even the world's strongest human chess players.

Thus I created WraithAI and named the game as Ghostfleet. WraithAI features:

1. Monte Carlo Simulation with Probability heatmaps: Before every turn WraithAI samples 800 possible enemy fleet configurations and aggregates them into a probability heatmap. It identifies the most likely locations of the enemy ships.

2. Bayesian Inference: After every shot it updates its beliefs and uses the information gain to draw a new heatmap. When two cells look equally likely WraithAI picks the one whose result would tell more about the hidden enemy fleet for its next turn.

3. Adaptive Strategy & defense: It adjusts its aggression based on the state of the game and has a mechanism which resists common search strategies.

I would genuinely like to know how people can find patterns in its behavior. Can you outsmart & beat WraithAI?

Ghostfleet also has multiplayer mode so you can play with your friends. There is a matchmaking component called TownSquare at the bottom through which you can share room codes with other players.

You can play directly in your browser:

1. Play against WraithAI: https://ghostfleet.in/play?mode=wraithAI

2. Ghostfleet: https://ghostfleet.in/

3. WraithAI Technical breakdown: https://ghostfleet.in/wraith-ai

records.title: Show HN: Cashcraft – free precise budgeting without categories
records.author: automattf
records.storyText:
Hi HN! I'm Matthew, a software engineer tired of paid budgeting apps doing fuzzy averages and making me categorize every card swipe.

Example: which category is Rent on the 1st? Which category is my $114 "Valuemart" purchase last week? It doesn't matter IMO. What matters is that Rent repeats every 1st, I have $218 left for spending until Friday, and I can contribute $500 to my Roth IRA next paycheck and have $2,000 left in that account.

Bills just cost what they cost, and I need to see exactly when they will come out and how much money that leaves me on that day.

For spending, I just move a hunk of cash to a separate "safe to spend" account every Friday and try not to blow through it. This means I can see exactly when spending money will come out too, and how much money that leaves me. I might spend more on gas this week and more for the party next week; there's no 'normal' week. It sounds simple, but it took me years of trial and error to find this system that consistently works for me and make a halfway-decent app to track it.

Cashcraft is free, and doesn't require an account to start locally. If you do sign up, your data is end-to-end encrypted. Bank sync is built but not public yet, because it costs money via Plaid, but you can import transactions from your bank. I might add it as a paid feature later. I wish bank sync could be free, but integrating with 100s of legacy bank systems necessarily costs Plaid money, which makes them charge implementers money.

If you're interested, give it a try and let me know what you like or don't about it. I'd like to improve it. Thank you!

records.author: garrinm
records.storyText:
Jam is a music making game that runs in the browser. You start with one instrument, and you write parts on a piano roll. Create your own music or play gigs (levels) to ear coin and buy more gear. Each gig is built around one musical idea, so you pick up some music knowledge as you go. Friends can join your studio with a link and write parts alongside you.

In my other Show HNs I've always come with my own code. In this case I didn't write the code, but I'm still proud of the outcome and I hope some of you will enjoy it too.

The audio code is Rust/WASM running in a worklet. This is the part I had prior experience in, and it's been fun getting that into a browser. The instruments are decent and the signal chains hold their own. The front end is the agent's own design in three.js. The optimization work there was interesting because of how busy the UI gets and how many elements come into view. I focused on measuring React renders per interaction, instruction counts for the audio engine, load times and frame times. The result is something that runs decently even on a phone.

This is a beta: feedback, comments and criticisms are all welcome. You can get into the game with no signup, and if you want to save your progress you'll be prompted to enter an email address.

records.storyText:
I started to meal prep a few months ago, and loved it because it saves me time and frees my mind. Also I spend way less ordering food when I don't know what to eat, which is often. But I got tired of looking for recipes in books and websites that I could not adapt to myself.

I tried using ChatGPT and Claude with nice prompts to make my meal plans, and the first results were promising, but when I went to the kitchen to make them, I realized that they were anything but consistent: missing ingredients, absurd quantities, missing steps, inconsistent shopping lists... inconsistencies everywhere. And I had to go back and forth 1000 times on rebuilding prompts every time.

I am a developer, so I decided to build a tool on my own, for myself, trying to fix in code what AI keeps getting wrong: I left AI do the creative part, and the code take care of reliability. And it keeps getting better, since it has been evolving ever since.

Finally I decided to make this Free App to see if other people wanted to try it and if it would solve the same issue for anyone else.

Any feedback is appreciated, and if you meal prep, I hope you like it!

I look up a lot at the sky at night and made this because I wanted to better understand what is up there.

Orbital shows all 32,000+ tracked objects at their current positions: about 17,000 working satellites, 2,800 dead ones, 2,200 spent rocket bodies and 10,700 pieces of debris.

Each is color coded, can be switched off, and can be "clicked" to follow. For the well-known ones it pulls up a real photo (where available), what it is for, and when it stopped working.

There is an animation that shows launch history from 1957 to today. When you first visit, click on the "Watch 1957 → today" button to see the animation.

You can also "fly out" to the solar system and see the planets, moons, comets and spacecraft further out there.

My orbit data comes from Space-Track. I also pull from CelesTrak to determine which satellites are currently active.

It is a static site on GitHub Pages (currently) with no backend, no accounts, and no ads. It also installs as an app and reopens offline.

I wrote it with Claude Code doing most of the implementation. I will provide the link to the source if you want it.

I would like to hear what you think about it. Specifically, what is confusing on a first visit, and what would make you come back to it. And anything else constructive you would like to share.

records.title: Show HN: Forbear - React-style native UI in C; a calculator in 3.6MB, 10MB RAM
records.author: Gabrielmfern
records.storyText:
Hello! Looking to share forbear, a immediate mode GUI library that looks like the web, has a React-like DX and is as fast as possible.

I've already built a real program (https://github.com/gabrielmfern/calculator) to stress it, and the binary is only 3.6MB, the first frame shows up in ~300ms, it uses 10.5MB of working set memory, and it's all 1,155 lines of code.

It can be used with Jai (Jonathan Blow's private beta programming language), and also from C or any C-compatible language.

On Linux and macOS:

  curl -fsSL https://forbear.dev/quick-start.sh | sh
On Windows:

records.title: Show HN: Online curling game/SIM with Three.js
records.author: nrjames
records.storyText:
Hello!

One of my hobbies is curling in a league with the local curling club. From time to time, there's a setup of stones that is tricky and interesting to contemplate from a strategic perspective. A while back, I started working on a three.js-based curling simulator that would enable me to recreate situations from my league games and then try different shots.

As you may know, curling is notoriously tricky from a physics perspective. There are a variety of papers out there about this, including this one, which is one of the more recent dives into understanding why stones curl the way they do: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-018-26595-y

Anyhow, with the help of Claude Code, I pulled together the work and converted the quick-and-dirty sim into a game you can play online. It's still a bit more of a sim than a game, perhaps, but it can be fun to play as a game.

Curling often is referred to as "chess on ice" because there's more strategy in choosing shots and playing ends than there would appear to be at first glance. The primary challenge of turning this into a game has been trying to figure out how to provide the computer player both with a policy for game and end-level strategy while also having it evaluate the tactical choices that have to be made for each shot.

For example, when would the computer try to blank (no points scored) an end deliberately so that it can retain hammer (last stone thrown) in the subsequent end? When should it throw a low vs. high center or corner guard in an attempt to make up a point deficit? When should it try to steal points from the hammer team vs. throwing protective stones that hold the hammer team to one point?

It's a fun side project for me, so I thought you all might enjoy giving it a shot. :)

p.s. In a game, if you go into the settings, you can turn on debug mode, which will reveal a panel on the right with a variety of (currently-undocumented) parameters you can tweak.

records.title: Show HN: Nunya – A "digital privacy screen" that makes text illegible from afar
records.author: magicmarc
records.storyText:
Hello! I'm Marc.

I've built "Nunya", which is a sort of "digital privacy screen".

It redraws text to make it readable when looking at your monitor or phone from a normal distance, while making it hard to read by someone who might be looking over your shoulder.

It's based on “hybrid images” like the famous Einstein/Monroe image (from the paper at https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1141911.1141919) and I thought it'd make a great way to mask text on your phone that you don't want someone nearby reading.

I particularly spent time on the transition - I wanted the text to be incredibly legible when close, but incredibly illegible when being far, and tried to optimise for a minimal transition between the two.

Demos can be seen at my site for it here: https://usenunya.com

I first released this over ten years ago as "PrivacyMessage" (my app names have definitely improved) when Apple first allowed iMessage apps. This was my first app geared towards the general market as I've spent the last 13 years developing iOS apps for a fairly niche market.

I'm happy to have brought it back as “Nunya”, and have currently made it available in three forms:

- Nunya for Messages (iPhone)

I first remade my iMessage app and gave it a bit more polish. It's free for 5 sends, and then $4.99 for a permanent unlock.

- Potfolio (iPhone)

I then figured Nunya would make for a great flagship feature in a "wealth tracking" finance app I was already working on, so anyone who might glance at your phone when on public transport can't quite see your bank balances. It's currently free (though I might add some new features with IAPs to it later).

- Nunya for Chrome

A friend then suggested it'd make for a great Chrome extension to be used on all sites. It's free to hide money amounts, and £10 (around $13) to unlock it to work with more (bank details, bitcoin addresses, etc). You can try it here: https://usenunya.com/chrome

This is my first real attempt at making apps for a wider market. It's also my very first Chrome extension, and I'm not entirely sure how best to price each of these, nor how to best gate their features. I don't particularly like subscriptions if I can avoid them.

I'm curious to hear any thoughts. Particularly: do you think these pricing models are reasonable? I also wonder if Nunya would make for a good feature elsewhere. With more staff working remotely who might be in transit or in cafes, I can imagine businesses could be keen for their staff to use it on more sensitive data. Does that seem plausible?

Thanks all.

records.title: Show HN: HyprMac: Keyboard-driven tiling window manager for macOS
records.author: zachtgray
records.storyText:
HyprMac is an app organizer and workspace manager for macOS, inspired by Hyprland on Linux. Every time I open a new app, it instantly positions itself nicely in a tiled layout alongside my other apps on screen. By repurposing the Caps Lock key (who, let's face it, never got much use anyways) into the Hypr key, I now can use that one button to traverse across windows, swap apps around, switch workspaces, and a ton of other awesome stuff. If you ever forget a shortcut, Hypr + K shows you the whole list.

On top of that, there are a few extras I've come to rely on. An overview shows all your workspaces at once. A scratchpad holds apps you want nearby but out of the way. Apps that don't tile revert to the typical macOS behavior, which we call 'floating windows.' These sit on top of the tiled apps and are free to drag around on top of workspaces. It also features a real settings UI, accessible from the menu bar, so you don't spend time digging around for config files.

I'm a software developer and a macOS power user. For the last 15 years, I've pretty much only used a Mac for everything. I've tried Windows here and there, but these days I also have a Linux PC alongside my Mac. I went through a few distributions before I came across Omarchy (amazing distro btw), which uses Hyprland to automatically tile windows. By just learning a few shortcuts you can completely manage all your apps across a number of workspaces instantly. I fell in love, and I knew I had to have that experience on my Mac. I poked around at a few of the options, but none of them really did exactly what I had in mind. Thus, HyprMac was born.

To install HyprMac, follow the guide at https://hyprmac.app/guides/install/ (Homebrew or the DMG).

There is, though, the harsh reality of macOS. All window managers that keep SIP enabled, HyprMac included, play under the same constraints of fighting the native macOS window manager. There are some edge cases where macOS doesn't play nicely with it. Hypr + P will be your friend here, to toggle tiling so you can quickly do what needs to be done before resuming again. There are built in safeguards to help with this, like HyprMac remembering which apps don't tile, and the ability to manually prevent certain apps from ever trying to tile.

Any and all bug reports, PRs, GitHub issues, hate mail, are welcome! I really hope you enjoy what I, alongside many kind developers on GitHub who are always sharing ideas and code, have built!

records.title: Show HN: Prediction market competition where only agents can trade
records.author: TNNick
records.storyText:
Hi HN. I’ve been working on a project called Vaticin (with an i). Interested in your feedback.

Vaticin is a prediction market competition platform where only agents are allowed to make wagers. Humans can’t directly do so themselves. There’s no real-money wagering involved. Vaticin is built for competition, research, and education.

Every Monday morning, our LLM generates about 300 yes/no prediction questions across six categories: sports, finance, tech, entertainment, geopolitics, and science. The competition window runs Monday through Saturday, although some predictions won’t resolve for several weeks later. Agents take positions/allocations throughout the week, and then wagering locks on Saturday. Odds are live/dynamic and update with every new wager. Then a new competition cycle starts the next Monday.

We have a live leaderboard that refreshes as our LLM resolves prediction questions each night (with human moderation of resolutions).

Recognizing the value of existing prediction market competition platforms, we wanted to focus on forecasting models that are not only well-calibrated, but also make good market decisions and integrate game theory into their strategy. On Vaticin, agents have to decide which markets to take positions on, when to take a position, and how much to allocate. With the dynamic odds, agents have to adapt throughout the competition cycle. Vaticin measures more than raw prediction accuracy.

We built a few ways to build an agent. Beginners can use our no-code “agent builder” and choose which forecasting parameters/strategies they want to use, then Vaticin codes their agent, shows the user the code, but allows them to edit the code. I hope it will help beginners learn more about coding and AI agents. More experienced builders can connect their own agents through an API.

We added private tournaments, where users can create their own tournaments with their own prediction questions and fantasy tournaments where “captains” can recruit a team of agents from other users. Separate leaderboards.

We’re still building, and recognize the site isn’t “perfect” yet, but the weekly competitions/private tournaments/fantasy tournaments are live.

I’d really appreciate feedback on a few things:

- Is Vaticin’s market-based/gamified format different enough from existing forecasting competitions to be relevant?

- How would you score and rank agents over the long term? We use metrics like Brier score vs the market with adjustments for wager sample size. What else should we consider?

- What features would make you interested in entering an agent into the competition?

- Would private/custom tournaments be useful for classes, research groups, hackathons, or recruiting?

- How should we discourage human users from hand-picking their “autonomous” agents’ bets? For Vaticin-hosted agents we can log every code edit, but we aren’t sure how to integrate that into the agent ratings. For self-hosted agents we can’t track this at all. Any insight into how other bot leagues (poker, algo trading, etc) handle this?

Leaderboard: https://www.vaticin.ai/leaderboard

Note: Early in the competition week, the leaderboard will show many agents at or close to their starting 100,000-token balance because a lot of positions haven't been resolved yet (and tokens are deducted when a wager is made, so the leaderboard will show many agents with less than their initial 100,000 token allocation).

Markets: https://www.vaticin.ai/markets

Note: The prediction questions are only visible when the weekly competition cycle is open, so if you visit on the weekend that page may be empty. You can pull up prior weeks’ predictions to take a look.

Agent builder: https://www.vaticin.ai/build-an-agent

Everything is free right now. No ads.

Happy to answer questions. Thanks for any feedback, good or bad.

Thanks!

records.title: Show HN: Wikipedia Current Event Portal as an Actual Newspaper (and in RSS)
records.author: aeonfr
records.storyText:
I wanted to diversify the sources of my RSS feeds, and realized the Wikipedia Current Events portal (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portal:Current_events) contains events that sometimes other sources missed.

I decided to create an RSS feed for it, but after a while I realized the entries are sometimes too long and are truncated in the RSS title, and some entries don't have a proper article linked to them so it was not possible to properly render a title and link for each RSS feed.

So I ended up creating a web portal to check the news. The site is static and updates around 2 times a day.

I added some nice features like crawling the linked sources and showing the original news websites title and image (this only works if the site provides og: tags and accepts connections from crawlers), and grouping related articles visually.

Hope you find this useful, or at least, interesting.

As attributed in the footer of the page:

"Unofficial project, not affiliated with the Wikimedia Foundation. The text comes from Wikipedia contributors and is available under the CC BY-SA 4.0 license; every entry links to the source article and its page history."

records.title: Show HN: Fdroid Feed Manager and API
records.author: npodbielski
records.storyText:
Hi guys. I had an idea to wrote API and some nice WebUI for Fdroid private feed for Android APKs for quite some time. I have some internal applications that I want to share with my family (i.e. smart home management app). First I had just bunch of static files that were managed by my GitLab instance but at some point it broke.

Then with growing number of applications and packages and no possibility of managing them easily (I think Fdroid tools are unnecessarily complicated) it was too much to do by hand. With coding agents I decided to try it out and write an application entirely by agent (as kind of experiment) it was usable but quite buggy. And costly.

After that I fixed bugs with local model, cleaned up code, added tests, tested it for few weeks myself with Fdroid clients on multiple phones and other devices. It is working and I decided to share it with community.

It us an API wrapping Fdroid python packages for managing Fdroid feed, signing APKs and etc. It supports API keys that I am feeding to my CI to upload new APKs after the build. It allows to:

- add, update and remove applications

- manages their keys so you do not have to

- allows to add description and icons

- allows to add (with release changes) and remove releases of applications

- manages versions of next release

It is designed to be integrated with SSO of your choice, because having SSO for your self hosted applications seems much better idea than each of local applications to manage it itself.

Links:

https://github.com/npodbielski/FdroidManager

https://hub.docker.com/r/npodbielski/fdroidmgr/tags

I hope it can be of use for more people.

records.title: Show HN: Local Graph for Your Agents
records.author: vmikhailov
records.storyText:
We all use different agentic systems, bots, chats, and so on. One day I realized that I need to copy context between the apps. It is annoying.

So I created a trivial local MCP which sits on top of SQLite and exposes Cypher so LLM can query anything. Also LLM can define a schema if it understands it needs new nodes or edges.

How do I use it: 1. I've scanned all my documents and stored passports, driver licences and all kind of contracts for my apartment, insurance and so on. And not only mine - the entire family. 2. I've extracted all the key date and values. Also gemini extracted all the personal relations. Like "Alex is-a-child-of Bob". "Bob is-married-to Anna". So i can ask "give me a passport number of my son" and it gives it back instantly. It might not be a big deal, but it is very convenient. 3. It stores all the projects I'm working on, key steps and decisions. 4. And the most important thing - it works from anywhere. I can ask Hermes i telegram to remind me when my insurance ends or I can reference my project in ClaudeCode just by name and it will get the entire history from Antigravity.

I would be happy if you guys find it useful.

records.title: Show HN: An open-source harness for Android devs in the terminal
records.author: gerardosuarez
records.storyText:
This open-source TUI and CLI allows running the workflows that android devs run every day without leaving the terminal and each one in their own worktree.

You can see the agents working in a control pane with different status. The TUI will inform you when it needs your help.

You can: 1. Create a Pull Request from a ticket, the harness does a plan -> code -> review workflow. You can decide the model per state. 2. Auto fix the ticket comments, the harness fetches the PR comments and show it in the dashboard. You can previsualize and approve or request a new fix. 3. Review the diff, the TUI has a beauty diff viewer so you can review the code without leaving the terminal. 4. Open the worktree in Android Studio or claude code directly from the TUI. 5. Permission and budget management: you can auto approve comments or approve once. You can also set a spend limit per stage.

It is optimized for android: 1. Only one agent at a time can take control of the emulator. 2. The worktree creation, all git operations and PR information is deterministic and handled by the harness taking into consideration how Android projects are built. 3. Open the worktree in Android Studio. 4. Open the emulator from the TUI.

Caveats: For now it only works for Claude Code.

records.title: Show HN: It's Raining Somewhere – hear live simulated weather anywhere on Earth
records.author: DanielSuncost
records.storyText:
I like listening to rain and I like maps, so I built a physics-based simulator of how rain sounds on different surfaces and linked it up to a live weather map.

You can pick any place on the map and play what the rain there would sound like right now, driven by live weather data. It grew into a whole soundscape: thunder, wind, seasonally appropriate birds, insects, frogs, the sea, vehicles and other urban sounds. The sound is binaural, so with headphones it has some spatial depth.

Only the birds are recordings (from xeno-canto, with attribution). Every other environmental sound is synthesized in your browser by a C++ engine compiled WebAssembly.

There's also a live radio that tunes to real local stations near wherever you are on the map. It gets mixed with the environmental sounds and you can adjust it to sound like it's coming from far away. Nearby storms can add crackle to the radio signal.

The radar map comes from my own tile server. It uses raw public radar data where available and falls back to satellite otherwise.

I'd love to hear feedback!
